title: 2021 Locust × Ground Cover
text:
We would like to see how density is influenced by ground cover. To do this I am building a generalized additive model (family: tweedie). Following this form:
The generalized additive model (GAM) fitted is:
\[
\begin{align*}
\text{ose\_count}_i = \\
  &\alpha + \\
  &+ f(\text{percent\_ground\_cover}_i,\, \text{region\_treat}_i) +  \\
  &+ b_{\text{farmer}_i} + \\
  &+ \varepsilon_i
\end{align*}
\]
where:
The model diagnostics look pretty good! I tried to build a poisson model, but the data was overdispersed. Instead I went with a tweedie model which does a pretty good job at handling this type of data:
However, I am not able to reproduce the smooths seen in the manuscript sent to me. This is likely due to data differences as I am not sure what was included in the initial modeling approach. Roughly we can see similiar trends in Kaffrine, Fatick, and Saint Louis. But Thies definitely has a different trend. Additionally, there seems to be different trends between control and fertilized treatments as comapred to the current plots in the manuscript. Not sure what to think here.

Doesnt look too strong, but lets model. I will hold the following variables as random effects: farmer number, region, and mission_number. Holding mission_number as a random effect can help with puesodreplication.

title: Fertilization Effects on Oedaleus senegalensis and Millet Yield in Senegal
text:
This site presents a reproducible analysis of the 2021 Oedaleus senegalensis (OSE) dataset, collected across four regions of Senegal: Fatick, Kaffrine, Thiès, and Saint-Louis. The study examined how fertilizer application influences grasshopper densities and millet yield, while also providing insights into OSE’s regional dynamics and distribution along a rainfall gradient.
The analyses and figures here build on previous work from our Scientific Reports paper, applying similar statistical frameworks to an expanded dataset that includes additional regions and survey rounds. All scripts, data processing, and visualizations are documented in this Quarto project for transparency and reproducibility.

title: Fertilization Effects on Oedaleus senegalensis and Millet Yield in Senegal
text:
This site presents a reproducible analysis of the 2021 Oedaleus senegalensis (OSE) dataset, collected across four regions of Senegal: Fatick, Kaffrine, Thiès, and Saint-Louis. The study examined how fertilizer application influences grasshopper densities and millet yield, while also providing insights into OSE’s regional dynamics and distribution along a rainfall gradient.
The analyses and figures here build on previous work from our Scientific Reports paper, applying similar statistical frameworks to an expanded dataset that includes additional regions and survey rounds. All scripts, data processing, and visualizations are documented in this Quarto project for transparency and reproducibility.

title: Fertilization Effects on Oedaleus senegalensis and Millet Yield in Senegal
text:
Study Background
During the 2021 growing season (July–October), 250 farmers participated in a paired-field experiment where each managed:

One fertilized field receiving 150 kg each of NPK and urea.
One non-fertilized control field.

Each field was surveyed three times to record:

Grasshopper density and developmental stage
Vegetation cover and temperature
Millet yield at harvest

In total, the survey covered 500 ha across 1,500 sampling points. The Saint-Louis region, which experienced extreme dryness that year, was only sampled twice due to field abandonment.

title: Fertilization Effects on Oedaleus senegalensis and Millet Yield in Senegal

title: 2021 Yield × Treatment × Region Results
text:
Goal
This analysis examines how fertilization influences millet yield across different regions. We expect to see regional differences in fertilizer response.


Raw data visualization
It is fairly obvious that fertilization influences millet yield. It is interesting to see the regional differences. It appears that Thies has a much strong response to fertilization than farms at Fatick or Kaffrine. Or at least the variation is dramatically less.











Modeling
This model formula will be similar to locust density by treatment x region. I will hold farmer as a random effect. So the model formula looks like this:
As can be seen in the modeled results below, fertilization significantly improved yield across the board. For whatever reason, Thies had lower yield unfertilized but also saw the biggest incase in yield when fertilized.

Goal
How is yield millet influenced by temperature during the growing season? This may be overkill, but I thought I would show this as well since the data has already been collected.


Raw data visualization
So I will calculate the mean and sd temperature and plot against yield to see if there are any interesting trends.









Not sure what to think about the potential non-linear relationship with yield x temperature. It might not be significant anyway. Happy to go further here if y’all are interested but for now I will leave it.

title: 2021 Locust × Temperature
text:
Overview
I checked how temperature varied across missions and regions. Fatick heated up through the sampling period, but Kaffrine, Thies, and Saint Louis were more stable. Saint Louis was generally colder than the other regions.
I then ran a GAM with a flexible smooth for temperature by region, including mission number and farmer as random effects. The trends were pretty similar to the original model, with the exception of some odd patterns at cooler temps.
To simplify, I also ran a model with temperature as the main variable and region/mission as random effects. In this case, both region and mission number came up significant for explaining OSE counts, but temperature and farmer had little effect.
Overall, it seems like temperature at the time of the survey isn’t a real driver for OSE counts once you control for region and mission—suggesting most of any pattern is noise or an artifact of timing/activity. I’m inclined to say temperature doesn’t need to be a focus in the main model, but happy to dig further if needed.









It looks like Fatick became hotter through the sampling period. Kaffrine, Thies, and Saint Louis seem more consistent between missions. Saint louis is definitely colder than the other three regions. So I would expect with the exception of Fatick, adding mission number to the model will not really add anything different.
Lets create the same model above with mission number included:









Seems like very similiar trends to the original model with the exception of more weird patterns in cooler temperatures.
